# 3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation

Valuation with multiples of comparable companies; how the P/E ratio relates to growth, ROE and the cost of equity; EV/EBITDA, price-to-book and price-to-sales, and keeping numerator and denominator consistent; the P/E of cyclical companies; CAPE and the valuation of the whole market.

Key file: https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/ai/en/lessons/3.11-key.md

## Valuation with multiples

The methods of Lesson 3.9, "Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-9-equity-valuation-ddm/ and Lesson 3.10, "Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-10-equity-valuation-dcf/ estimate future cash flows directly. In practice, relative valuation is used more often: find a group of companies with similar businesses (comparable companies), compute the ratio of their price to earnings, revenue or book value (a multiple), and multiply the target company's corresponding number by this multiple.

The most common multiple is the **price-earnings ratio** (P/E): price divided by earnings per share. Computed with the last 12 months of earnings it is the trailing P/E; with analysts' forecast earnings for the next 12 months it is the forward P/E.

Relative valuation is simple and intuitive, and it reflects the market's current price level directly. But it rests on two conditions: the comparable companies really are similar to the target in growth, risk and profitability, and the market prices the comparable companies reasonably. If a whole industry is overvalued, a value based on industry multiples is overvalued too.

## What the P/E ratio means

Multiples are not a method separate from DCF; they carry assumptions about growth and risk. From the Gordon model (Gordon growth model), next year's dividend is $D_1 = (1 - b)E_1$, where $b$ is the retention ratio:

$$
\frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1 - b}{r - g}
$$

So the forward P/E depends on three factors: the payout ratio, the cost of equity $r$ and the growth rate $g$. Other things equal, faster growth and lower risk (lower $r$) mean a higher P/E. Growth in turn depends on the return on reinvestment (sustainable growth rate): Exercises Question 1 derives how the P/E depends on ROE.

The inverse of the P/E, $\frac{E_1}{P_0}$, is the earnings yield.

## Other multiples

- **EV/EBITDA**: enterprise value divided by EBITDA. The numerator includes equity and debt, and the denominator is profit before interest; both belong to all investors, so the ratio is unaffected by capital structure, and also by depreciation policy. It is often used to compare companies with different debt levels. But it ignores capital spending: a capital-intensive company has a high EBITDA, but much of it must go into replacing equipment.
- **Price-to-book ratio** (P/B): price divided by book equity per share. It suits companies whose assets are mainly financial and carried close to market value, such as banks and insurers. How P/B relates to ROE and the cost of equity is in Exercises Question 2.
- **Price-to-sales ratio** (P/S): market value of equity divided by revenue. It can be used for companies with negative or very unstable profit, but revenue is not profit, so it must be read together with margins (Exercises Question 3).

In any multiple, numerator and denominator must belong to the same investors: equity value (price, market value) goes with numbers that belong to shareholders (net income, book equity), and enterprise value goes with numbers that belong to all investors (EBITDA, EBIT; revenue is also commonly divided into enterprise value).

## Cyclical companies and CAPE

The profits of cyclical companies such as steel, automobiles and semiconductors swing widely with the business cycle, while their prices reflect long-run value and move much less. Then the current P/E can mislead. Figure 4-1 uses a simplified example.

**Figure 4-1** A cyclical company's price stays at 100, while its annual earnings move around 5 in an 8-year cycle. P/E uses current earnings; CAPE uses the average earnings of the last 10 years.
- This figure has no drawing instructions yet: give the learner the link to the web page and say what to change and what to observe.
- What the learner should observe: First set the amplitude of the earnings cycle to 0, then raise it step by step and compare how the two lines change; notice at which stage of the earnings cycle the P/E is highest.
- Interactive figure on the web page (the learner can also open it): https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-11-relative-valuation/#fig-4-1

> **Check question C4**
> 
> In Figure 4-1, set the amplitude of the earnings cycle to 0.5. When is a cyclical company's P/E highest?
> 
> (A) When earnings are at their peak
> (B) When earnings are at their trough
> (C) When earnings grow fastest
> (D) It does not depend on the cycle
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

For the stock market as a whole, Shiller proposed replacing current earnings with the average inflation-adjusted earnings of the past 10 years; this is the **cyclically adjusted P/E** (CAPE), also called the Shiller P/E. In Shiller's data, the CAPE of the S&P 500 has averaged about 17 since 1881 and reached a record of about 44 in December 1999; from late 2025 into 2026 it has been roughly between 39 and 41.

Research finds that when CAPE is high, the stock market's average real return over the following 10 years tends to be low. But the relation is far from exact: CAPE can stay very high for years, and using it to time purchases and sales works poorly. Whether CAPE can be used to estimate long-run expected returns, and what to watch for, is in Exercises Question 4; Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/ discusses estimating long-run expected returns more systematically.

## Summary

- Relative valuation multiplies the target's earnings, revenue or book value by the multiple of comparable companies; this assumes the comparables really are similar and the market prices them reasonably.
- Forward P/E $\frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1 - b}{r - g}$: it depends on the payout ratio, the cost of equity and the growth rate.
- EV/EBITDA is unaffected by capital structure and depreciation policy but ignores capital spending; P/B suits banks and other financial companies; P/S must be read with margins. Numerator and denominator must belong to the same investors.
- The current P/E of cyclical companies misleads; CAPE uses 10-year average real earnings and is negatively related to average returns over the next 10 years, but cannot be used to time the market precisely.

## Exercises

Assign them after the lesson. Answers and grading points are in the key file.

**Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)**

(a) From $\frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1 - b}{r - g}$ and $g = b \times \text{ROE}$, write the forward P/E as a function of $g$, ROE and $r$.
(b) The cost of equity is 9% and growth 4%. What is the justified P/E with an ROE of 20% and of 9%? Why do the P/Es differ when growth is the same?

**Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)**

One can show that under the Gordon model's assumptions, $\frac{P_0}{B_0} = \frac{\text{ROE} - g}{r - g}$, where $B_0$ is book equity per share.
(a) A bank has a cost of equity of 10% and long-run growth of 4%. What is the justified P/B with an ROE of 12% and of 8%?
(b) Why do many banks trade below book value per share for long periods? Does this mean they are undervalued?

**Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)**

Companies A and B both have a P/S of 2. A's net margin is 20% and B's is 2%.
(a) What is each company's P/E?
(b) An analyst says: "A and B have the same P/S, so they are valued equally high." If the market believes B's P/E will end up equal to A's, what net margin does the price paid for B imply that B must reach? Evaluate the analyst's statement.

**Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)**

A rough view holds that the inverse of CAPE (the cyclically adjusted earnings yield) approximates the stock market's long-run real expected return.
(a) With a CAPE of 36 and of 15, what long-run real expected return does this approximation give?
(b) Give two reasons why today's CAPE may not be directly comparable with CAPE decades ago. Does each reason make today's CAPE look higher or lower than the true level of valuation?
